item.title: C Language: Zero-Sized Array Legality and Practical Alternatives
item.description:
“C Language: Zero-Sized Array Legality and Practical Alternatives”

What is the definitive stance of the C programming language standard regarding arrays declared with a size of zero? Furthermore, how do common compiler extensions and established programming idioms, such as the “struct hack,” interact with this constraint?

The initial assessment, confirmed by the C standard (ISO 9899:2011 6.7.6.2 ), is quite strict:

  1. Constant Expression Size: If an array dimension is a constant expression, its value must be greater than zero.
  2. Variable Length Arrays (VLAs): For VLAs, if the controlling expression evaluates to less than or equal to zero, the behavior is officially undefined. Compilers are obligated to adhere to this normative text. Using strict compilation flags like gcc -std=c99 -pedantic will reliably generate a warning for non-VLA zero-sized declarations.

item.title: Solved: How to Clarify JavaScript Parameter Passing Semantics
item.description:
“Solved: How to Clarify JavaScript Parameter Passing Semantics”

Let’s dive deep into various perspectives and practical examples to resolve this common source of perplexity for JavaScript developers.

The Core Concept: Call-by-Sharing

JavaScript fundamentally passes all arguments by value. However, the “value” passed depends on the type of data:

  1. Primitive Data Types (numbers, strings, booleans, null, undefined, symbols): The actual value is copied. Any changes to the parameter inside the function do not affect the original variable outside.
  2. Object Data Types (objects, arrays, functions): The value passed is a reference to the object. This means both the original variable and the function parameter point to the same object in memory. While you can modify the object’s properties through this reference, reassigning the parameter itself to a new object will not affect the original variable. This specific behavior is often termed call-by-sharing.

item.title: Solved: Should You Cast `malloc` in C? A Deep Dive into Memory Allocation Best Practices
item.description:
“Solved: Should You Cast malloc in C? A Deep Dive into Memory Allocation Best Practices”

Is Casting malloc Redundant in C, and Why Might It Be Considered Harmful?

A prominent viewpoint in the C community suggests that casting malloc’s return value is not only unnecessary but can introduce issues. What are the specific reasons behind this perspective?

  1. Automatic Pointer Promotion: In C, a void * (which malloc returns) is automatically and safely promoted to any other pointer type during assignment. This implicit conversion is a fundamental language feature, making an explicit cast redundant.
  2. Code Clutter and Readability: Adding an explicit cast can introduce visual “clutter” to the code, potentially making it less straightforward to read, particularly when dealing with lengthy pointer types. This goes against the principle of writing concise and clear code.
  3. Repetitive Information: When you cast, you repeat the type information. This redundancy can lead to maintenance challenges. If the target pointer’s type changes, forgetting to update the cast will still compile, but it might lead to incorrect memory allocation sizes or logical errors that are difficult to debug.
  4. Masking Missing Headers (Pre-C99): In older C standards (before C99), if you omitted #include <stdlib.h>, the compiler might implicitly assume malloc returned an int. Assigning this int to a pointer without a cast would typically trigger a warning. However, adding an explicit cast would suppress this warning, effectively hiding a potential bug where int and pointer sizes differ, leading to undefined behavior or crashes. While modern compilers usually warn about undeclared functions regardless of the cast, the historical context highlights a potential risk.
